guide.title: Geriatrics
guide.lead: Older adults present quietly: a heart attack as weakness, sepsis without fever, a fracture after a 'simple' fall. Ask why they fell, what they take and what is new compared with their usual self. Never put new confusion down to age.

sections.title: Ageing changes what you see
rows: Stiffer, slower response; beta-blockers blunt tachycardia
A normal heart rate doesn't rule out shock; a 'normal' BP may be low for someone with hypertension
Pneumonia and aspiration; they desaturate quickly
Slow subdural bleeds days after minor falls, especially on anticoagulants
Sepsis may come without fever, or with hypothermia
Fractures and pressure injuries from small forces: pad everything

sections.title: Delirium, dementia or depression?
rows: Medical emergency: infection, drugs, hypoxia, glucose, urinary retention, pain
Chronic; but delirium often sits on top of it
notes: Ask the carer: is this new? Use the 4AT if your service has it.

steps.title: Why did they fall?
steps.text: Dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, fainting, new weakness, infection, medicines, or a trip. A fall is a symptom.

steps.title: Long lie
steps.text: On the floor for 1 hour or more: pressure injury, rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, dehydration, pneumonia.

steps.title: Injuries
steps.text: Hip (short, externally rotated leg: padded splint, no traction), wrist, ribs, head. On anticoagulants, any head strike goes to hospital even if they look well.

steps.title: Where to
steps.text: Age 65 or older with systolic below 110 mmHg is high-risk; anticoagulants are a moderate-risk factor (Field Triage 2021).

steps.title: Staying home?
steps.text: Only if the cause is clear and they can cope: hazards, help, a way to call. Refer per local pathway.

sections.title: Medicines to ask about (5 or more = polypharmacy)
items: Beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin: slow heart, blunted response to shock
Diuretics, ACE inhibitors: dehydration, abnormal sodium and potassium
Benzodiazepines, opioids, sleeping tablets: falls and confusion
Bring all the medicines or a list

sections.title: Elder abuse (about 1 in 6 people aged 60 or older, WHO)

groups.title: Signs
items: Injuries of different ages, grip marks on the arms
Missing glasses, hearing aids or dentures
Money or belongings controlled by someone else

groups.title: Do
items: Document what you see and hear
Report per local law (adult protective services)

sections.title: Advance directives
items: DNR (DNACPR): no CPR if they arrest. Still treat everything else – oxygen, pain, infection – unless the document says otherwise.
POLST, MOLST or local forms (such as ReSPECT) set the level of care: full, limited or comfort.
A valid document or the legal decision-maker outweighs other family wishes. Unsure? Start care and call medical direction.

items.label: Inferior STEMI
items.sub: Weakness, nausea or confusion may be the only symptom. 12-lead early.

items.label: Atrial fibrillation
items.sub: Common cause of falls, stroke and anticoagulant use.

items.label: Complete heart block
items.sub: Think of drugs: beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin.

quiz.q: 74-year-old with diabetes: sudden confusion and weakness, no chest pain, ST elevation in the anterior leads. This is:
options: An atypical presentation of acute MI
quiz.explanation: Older adults and people with diabetes often have no chest pain.

quiz.q: Nursing home: man with Alzheimer's, confused since yesterday and now seeing bugs on the wall. 'It's just his dementia.' You:
options: Treat as possible delirium: look for a medical cause and transport
quiz.explanation: New hallucinations and fluctuating attention suggest delirium.

quiz.q: 88-year-old on the floor for 'a day or two', confused, red areas on the buttocks and heels. Main concern?
options: Long-lie complications: rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, dehydration, hypothermia, pneumonia
A glass of water and help up

quiz.q: 76-year-old with heart failure, COPD and AF: weak, 'not right', BP 96/58, HR 110, RR 24, SpO₂ 89%, no fever. Suspect:
options: Sepsis: fever is often absent in older adults

quiz.q: 85-year-old with a valid DNR has pneumonia and SpO₂ 85%. The family says 'do everything'. You:
options: Treat the pneumonia (oxygen, transport); withhold only CPR if she arrests
quiz.explanation: DNR means no CPR, not no care.

quiz.q: 92-year-old 'fell out of bed': grip-mark bruises on both wrists, black eye, withdrawn; son answers everything and refuses to leave. Suspect:
options: Elder abuse: speak with her alone and report
quiz.explanation: Patterned bruises and a controlling caregiver are red flags.

quiz.q: A 'long lie' is commonly defined as being on the floor for:
Bleeding older patient on a beta-blocker, HR 72, BP 104/60 (usually 160/90). You conclude:
options: Possible shock: the beta-blocker hides tachycardia and the BP is low for her

quiz.q: 80-year-old on an anticoagulant tripped and hit his head; feels fine. Best plan?
Suspected hip fracture (short, externally rotated leg). Splint with:
options: A padded splint or scoop with the legs secured together – no traction
A tight bandage over the hip
quiz.explanation: Traction is for mid-shaft femur fractures, not hips.

flashcards.question: Ageing changes that matter in EMS
flashcards.answer: Blunted heart rate response, less lung reserve, slower drug clearance, poor temperature control (less fever), brain shrinkage (subdural risk), thin skin, osteoporosis, sensory loss.

flashcards.question: MI in older adults
flashcards.answer: Often no chest pain: weakness, fainting, confusion, breathlessness, nausea or upper abdominal pain. Do a 12-lead early.

flashcards.question: Delirium, dementia, depression
flashcards.answer: Delirium: sudden, fluctuating attention, altered alertness – a medical emergency. Dementia: slow and progressive, alert. Depression: withdrawn, slowed, aware; ask about suicide.

flashcards.question: Falls in older adults
flashcards.answer: A symptom, not a diagnosis. Ask why: dizziness, heart, infection, stroke, medicines, hazards. Look for injury and long-lie complications.

flashcards.question: Polypharmacy
flashcards.answer: 5 or more medicines. Watch anticoagulants, beta-blockers, diuretics, insulin, sedatives and anticholinergics. Bring all medicines to hospital.

flashcards.question: Elder abuse
flashcards.answer: Physical, emotional, sexual, financial and neglect. Speak with the patient alone, document, and report according to local law.

flashcards.question: DNR vs POLST
flashcards.answer: DNR: no CPR if they arrest. POLST or equivalent (MOLST, ReSPECT): sets the wider level of care – full, limited or comfort.

flashcards.question: Dementia patient confused since this morning
flashcards.answer: Delirium until proven otherwise: infection (often urinary or chest), low glucose, low oxygen, drugs, retention, stroke. Transport.

critical.scenario: 80-year-old with diabetes and a coronary stent: weak, diarrhoea all morning, 'a stomach bug'. BP 88/54, HR 106, SpO₂ 94%, temperature normal; got lost in his own home.
critical.question: Stomach bug or more?

options.t: Shock with new confusion: think MI, sepsis or dehydration – 12-lead, glucose, IV, fluids per protocol, transport

critical.explanation: Absent chest pain and fever don't reassure in older adults.
critical.kpi: Recognizes atypical presentations and shock in older adults

critical.scenario: 90-year-old with Alzheimer's: fine yesterday, now agitated, picking at the air, 'spiders on the ceiling'. HR 104, warm, smell of urine; recurrent urinary infections. Staff suggest a sleeping pill.
critical.question: What is this?

options.t: Delirium, probably from infection: transport for assessment
Her usual dementia: give the sleeping pill
options.f: Sedation hides the cause and causes falls.

critical.explanation: Acute onset with fluctuating attention is delirium; urinary infection is a common trigger.

critical.scenario: 79-year-old fell; left leg short and externally rotated. She felt dizzy first, tired and with 'indigestion' for days. On a diuretic. BP 100/62. She says she'll just rest; her daughter disagrees.
critical.question: Plan?

options.t: Splint (no traction) and transport; look for the cause – 12-lead, glucose, electrolytes risk from the diuretic; assess capacity if she still refuses
Mechanical fall: splint, no further workup

options.f: A suspected hip fracture needs treatment; check capacity and explain risks.

options.t: Pain relief and leave her home
options.f: She can't walk on a broken hip.

critical.explanation: The hip is the injury; the dizziness may be an MI or arrhythmia.
critical.kpi: Investigates the medical cause of a fall while managing the injury
